input.content:
Step two of #73's route work, after #189 added the references. Every read of where
a flight goes now comes from the `Airport` rows it points at. The columns still
exist and still hold the same words, so **this is intended to be invisible** —
which is the point: it is what makes dropping them a migration rather than a
rewrite.

## What moved

`lib/flightRoute.ts` holds all of it, so no component learned about airports:

- `flightRouteInclude` — the relation a route-rendering query has to ask for.
  Spreads into a `select` as readily as an `include`.
- `withRouteLabels(flight)` — swaps the two columns for the airport labels, so
  every view keeps receiving a flight with `from` and `to` on it.
- `withLegRouteLabels(leg)` — the same for an itinerary leg.
- `flightRouteWhere(from, to)` — narrows a query by the airports rather than the
  prose.

Read sites migrated: search (both directions and the no-date branch), the
`/flights` status board, checkout, `/profile` history and points activity,
`/admin` recent bookings, `/admin/flights`, the booking-confirmation
notification, and the flight-status-change notification.

## The filter mattered as much as the render

`where: { from, to }` matched the label columns, so a search depended on two rows
spelling a place identically — and it kept the columns load-bearing long after
nothing rendered them. Those now filter on `fromAirportCode`/`toAirportCode`.

`flightRouteWhere` returns `null` when no airport answers to a name, and the
caller returns an empty result without querying. That is the same empty result
the label match gave, reached without a round trip — and `?from=` is a
user-controlled query parameter, so an unknown place is reachable.

`FlightSchedule.from`/`to` are deliberately untouched. That model has no airport
references; giving it them is separate work.

## Verification

The new database test writes a flight whose `from`/`to` columns say
`'Nowhere, Atlantis'` while its references say Seattle→Detroit, then searches. If
any read path still depends on the columns the flight either fails to come back
or comes back naming nowhere. Mutation-tested both ways: restoring the label
`where` fails two of the three cases, dropping `withRouteLabels` fails the third.

The status-notification unit test got the same treatment — its fixture's columns
now disagree with its airports, so the asserted message can only be right if the
code reads the references.

## What remains of #73

Step three drops `Flight.from` and `Flight.to`. The search URL still carries
labels; moving it to IATA codes is part of that step, and needs no compatibility
shim because the product has not launched.

gh issue create --title "Playwright silently reuses a stale dev server and reports a false failure" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Cost real time during #73 step 2a, and produced a **false regression signal** — verified against running code.

## Where

`playwright.config.ts:36-42`:

```ts
webServer: {
  command: 'npm run dev',
  url: 'http://localhost:3000',
  reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  ...
}
```

## What was observed

`e2e/admin.spec.ts:75` failed 3 runs out of 3 at line 244 — the flight was on the board but its status was never `Delayed`. The same spec passed on `HEAD`. That looks exactly like a regression in the branch, and I started bisecting the diff on that basis.

It was not a regression. A dev server left running from an earlier full-suite run was being reused, and it was serving stale output. After `pkill -f "next dev"`, the unchanged branch passed the spec 3 runs out of 3 and the full suite passed 28/28.

The bisect was worthless for a second reason that follows from the same line: because `webServer` runs `npm run dev`, `npm run build` before a Playwright run changes nothing about what is served. Reverting a file and rebuilding appeared to fix the failure when all it did was restart the server.

## Why it matters

Two failure modes, and the second is the dangerous one:

- A stale server makes a healthy branch look broken, which is where the time goes.
- A stale server can equally make a **broken branch look healthy** — the suite reports a pass against code that is not the code under test. `reuseExistingServer` is off in CI, so this is local-only, but local is where the pre-push decision gets made.

## Suggested fix

Either set `reuseExistingServer: false` outright, or keep the reuse and have the config assert the server is the current one — the runbook note alone is not enough, because nothing surfaces at the point of confusion. Related: #173, where the same line came up alongside e2e cleanup.
EOF

input.content:
Step two of #73's route work, after #189 added the references. Every read of where
a flight goes now comes from the `Airport` rows it points at. The columns still
exist and hold the same words, so **this is intended to be invisible** — which is
the point: it is what makes dropping them a migration rather than a rewrite.

## What moved

`lib/flightRoute.ts` holds all of it, so no component learned about airports:

- `flightRouteInclude` — the relation a route-rendering query asks for. Spreads
  into a `select` as readily as an `include`.
- `withRouteLabels(flight)` / `withLegRouteLabels(leg)` — swap the columns for the
  airport labels, so every view keeps receiving a flight with `from` and `to`.
- `flightRouteWhere(from, to)` — narrows a query by the airports, not the prose.

Read sites migrated: search (both directions and the dateless branch), the
`/flights` status board, checkout, `/profile` history and points activity,
`/admin`, `/admin/flights`, and both notification paths.

## The filter mattered as much as the render

`where: { from, to }` made a search depend on two rows spelling a place
identically, and kept the columns load-bearing regardless of what was displayed.
Those now filter on `fromAirportCode`/`toAirportCode`.

`flightRouteWhere` returns `null` when no airport answers to a name and the caller
returns empty without querying — the same result the label match gave. `?from=` is
user-controlled, so an unknown place is reachable.

`FlightSchedule.from`/`to` are untouched: that model has no references, and giving
it them is separate work.

## Verification, and what it caught

Two database suites write a flight whose columns say `'Nowhere, Atlantis'` while
its references say Seattle→Detroit — the only way to tell which source a page read,
since on every real row the two agree. Each of the seven converted paths was
mutation-tested by reverting it.

Three `verifier` rounds ran, and the first two found real holes rather than
confirming the work:

- **Five of the seven paths were covered by nothing.** They reverted cleanly with
  the entire suite green. That is the whole value of this change, so the page-level
  suite exists to close it.
- **My first version of that suite was vacuous for three of four cases** — the
  fixture departed outside the window `/admin/flights` renders, so assertions were
  passing on other seeded flights that happen to name Seattle. Fixed, with a
  flight-number assertion in every case as the non-vacuity guard (#155 again).
- **Asserting the route as text was still too weak.** A seeded reversed flight
  satisfies it on the fixture's behalf, and `/admin/flights` ships `FlightSchedule`
  prose carrying the same keys — that case was outright vacuous. The suite now
  finds the fixture's own flight object by flight number and reads the route off
  it.
- **The element walk was blind to host-element props**, so a column leaking through
  `title` or `aria-label` would have passed. It walks them now.
- Two further mutants survived and are now caught: dropping the `include` from the
  dateless search (a `TypeError` on every dateless search, reachable from the
  form), and re-attaching the relation objects to `updateFlightStatusAction`'s
  return value.

Final: `npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 48 database,
`npm run build`, and Playwright 28/28.

`ui-review` stood up a second server on the pre-change tree and diffed both:
text byte-identical across seven journeys at three viewports, 47 of 51 screenshot
pairs identical at 0.000% (the four are focus/hover timing).

One thing worth knowing: `admin.spec.ts` failed 3 runs of 3 and passed on `HEAD`,
which looked exactly like a regression. It was a stale dev server being reused —
filed as #196, because it can equally make a broken branch look healthy.

## Filed rather than fixed

#191 (the label→code and code→label mappings read different sources — the one
finding inside this slice's scope, and noted in `flightRouteWhere`), #192, #193,
#194, #195, #196, plus a note on #173.

## What remains of #73

Step three drops the columns. The search URL still carries labels; moving it to
IATA codes belongs there, and needs no compatibility shim because the product has
not launched.

input.content:
-- Stop storing a flight's route twice (#73).
--
-- `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` were free text that was simultaneously the
-- identity of a place and the words rendered to a customer. Editing the prose
-- silently repointed a route, and nothing stopped a flight naming somewhere no
-- airport exists.
--
-- The references arrived in #189 and every read moved to them in #197, so these
-- two columns have been write-only since. This removes the second answer to
-- "where does this flight go", which is what made the first one unreliable.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "from" TEXT, ADD COLUMN "to" TEXT;
--     UPDATE "Flight" f SET "from" = a."label"
--       FROM "Airport" a WHERE a."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode";
--     UPDATE "Flight" f SET "to" = a."label"
--       FROM "Airport" a WHERE a."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "from" SET NOT NULL,
--                          ALTER COLUMN "to" SET NOT NULL;
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260808120000_drop_flight_route_text';
--
-- The reversal reconstructs the labels from the airports, which is exactly what
-- the guard below proves they already are -- so nothing is lost that the
-- reversal cannot put back. It is safe against either version of the code:
-- old code reads columns that are there again, new code ignores them.
--
-- If the lock timeout aborts this, or the guard rejects the data, the migration
-- is marked failed and no later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260808120000_drop_flight_route_text

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- DROP COLUMN takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a table every search reads, and
-- `docker compose` starts the one-shot `migrate` service before recreating
-- `app`, so the previous container is still serving searches while this runs.
-- LOCAL, so it lasts only this transaction: a bare SET commits with the
-- migration and would impose itself on every migration authored afterwards
-- (#185).
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

-- Prove the columns are redundant before destroying them.
--
-- Dropping a column is the one change no later migration can undo from the
-- data, so this refuses to run while either column still says something the
-- airports do not. A disagreement means a label was edited after the flight was
-- written, and an operator has to decide which of the two is right -- silently
-- keeping the airport's answer would discard the other one unrecorded.
DO $$
DECLARE
    disagreements TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(
        format('%s: %L/%L vs %L/%L', "flightNumber", "from", "to", origin_label, destination_label),
        ', '
        ORDER BY "flightNumber"
    )
    INTO disagreements
    FROM (
        SELECT f."flightNumber", f."from", f."to",
               origin."label" AS origin_label,
               destination."label" AS destination_label
        FROM "Flight" f
        JOIN "Airport" origin ON origin."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode"
        JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"
        WHERE origin."label" <> f."from" OR destination."label" <> f."to"
        LIMIT 20
    ) AS mismatched;

    IF disagreements IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Flight.from/to disagree with the airports these flights reference: %. '
            'Each is a route that reads one way and books another. Decide which is '
            'right and correct the row or the airport label before dropping the columns.',
            disagreements;
    END IF;
END $$;

ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "from";
ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "to";

import pathlib, re, subprocess

files = subprocess.run(['npx','tsc','--noEmit'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
targets = sorted({l.split('(')[0] for l in files.splitlines() if l.startswith(('__tests__','e2e'))})

# Remove only a `from:`/`to:` pair that sits directly above an
# airportCodesForRoute spread inside a create -- the spread is what proves the
# lines belong to a Flight create rather than to a where clause or an assertion.
pattern = re.compile(r'^([ \t]*)from:[^\n]*\n[ \t]*to:[^\n]*\n(?=[ \t]*\.\.\.airportCodesForRoute\()', re.M)

for f in targets:
    p = pathlib.Path(f)
    if not p.exists(): continue
    s = p.read_text()
    new, n = pattern.subn('', s)
    if n: p.write_text(new); print(f'{n:2d} removed  {f}')

        FROM "Flight" f
        JOIN "Airport" origin ON origin."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode"
        JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"
        WHERE origin."label" <> f."from" OR destination."label" <> f."to"

new="""    SELECT string_agg(
        format('%s: %L/%L vs %L/%L', "flightNumber", "from", "to", origin_label, destination_label),

        -- that row, and it is the one row whose label cannot be reconstructed

        -- cannot satisfy. Both foreign keys are validated and RESTRICT, so
        -- reaching this needs replication-role trickery; it is handled anyway
        -- because the cost of being wrong here is an unrecoverable reversal.

        LEFT JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"

input.content:
The last structural piece of #73's route work, after #189 added the references and
#197 moved every read onto them. `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` have been write-only
since, and this removes them along with the four writers that filled them.

They were free text that was simultaneously the identity of a place and the words
shown to a customer, so editing the prose silently repointed a route and nothing
stopped a flight naming somewhere no airport exists.

## The migration

`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, a guard, then two `DROP COLUMN`s.

Dropping a column is the one change no later migration can undo from the data, so
the guard refuses to run while either column still says something the airports do
not. A disagreement means a label was edited after the flight was written, and an
operator has to decide which of the two is right — silently keeping the airport's
answer would discard the other one unrecorded.

Verified on scratch databases, by me and independently by the `verifier`:

- Two disagreeing rows and one agreeing: fails naming both bad ones and not the
  good one, columns survive, migration recorded failed, second deploy gives `P3009`
- `migrate resolve --rolled-back` → correct the rows → redeploy succeeds
- The reversal in the header reconstructs the labels exactly — 0 mismatches over 40
  rows
- From empty: `migrate deploy` + `db seed` gives 1412 flights, no orphan references,
  and `migrate diff` reports no difference
- Lock timeout applies: with a lock held from another session it aborts with `55P03`
  after ~3s and both columns survive, which also proves the file is one transaction
  and `SET LOCAL` is therefore not a silent no-op

The verifier found the guard's inner join let a flight referencing a **deleted**
airport slip past unchecked — and that row is precisely the one the reversal cannot
reconstruct, so it would fail on a `NOT NULL` it cannot satisfy. Reaching that state
needs `session_replication_role = replica`, since both FKs are validated and
`RESTRICT`, but the cost of being wrong is an unrecoverable reversal. It is a
`LEFT JOIN` with `IS DISTINCT FROM` now, and the message states the true total
rather than silently capping at 20.

## Removing the columns removed a cross-check

The whole-table invariant asserting the columns agreed with the airports is gone,
because the disagreement is now unstateable. That invariant was also what caught a
writer resolving a route to the *wrong* airports — and the verifier proved the gap
was real: reversing `airportCodesForRoute(from, to)` in `prisma/seed.ts` seeded 1412
flights onto backwards routes with all 608 unit and 48 database tests green.

The other three writers each fail a unit assertion on their create payload; the seed
was the only one without. It has one now, against the routes `FlightData` itself
names, covering 786 rows across both writers. Mutation-tested: the swap fails it.

## The two suites from #197 were rebuilt

Both were designed around a fixture whose columns contradicted its airports — the
only way to ask *which of two sources* a read used. That question is unaskable now,
so they assert the resolution itself: a page that forgets the relation gets
`undefined`, one that maps it wrongly gets the route backwards.

The fixture is Rio → Miami, because the seed flies Miami → Rio and not the reverse,
so no other row can satisfy the assertions on its behalf. The verifier confirmed
that against the seeded data (`GIG->MIA = 0`, `MIA->GIG = 157`) and re-ran the
mutation set: all 18 mutants killed, none that previously died now survives.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 49 database, `npm run
build`, Playwright 28/28 on a single cold run with no retries.

`ui-review` drove all eight journeys at three viewports, including creating a
schedule through the admin form — the path that writes new flights — and confirmed
the 30 generated occurrences render correctly, the unknown-place rejection is still
field-level and reports both fields at once, and no route renders `undefined`,
blank, or differently spaced.

## Filed rather than fixed

#198, #199, #200, #202, plus a comment on #193. And **#201**, which is not a
finding so much as a contradiction worth recording: `ui-review` measured focus
dropping to `<body>` after the schedule form rejects an unknown place, while the
jsdom test asserting that exact behaviour passes. Both can be true if a re-render
races the `requestAnimationFrame`. It needs a browser assertion to settle, and if
the browser is right then a test I added in #189 is asserting something
jsdom-specific.

## What remains of #73

The search URL still carries labels rather than IATA codes. That is the last piece,
it is independently shippable, and it needs no compatibility shim because the
product has not launched — so this PR does not close the issue.

def to_codes(m):
    global converted
    origin, destination = m.group(2), m.group(4)
    # Already a code (the new cases), or a place these fixtures never use.
    if origin not in CODES or destination not in CODES:
        return m.group(0)
    converted += 1
    return f'{m.group(1)}{CODES[origin]}{m.group(3)}{CODES[destination]}{m.group(5)}'

s = pattern.sub(to_codes, s)
print(f'param objects converted: {converted}')
p.write_text(s)

translation happens at the boundary. `buildFlightSearchUrl` writes codes,
`parseFlightSearchParams` reads them back as labels.

**No compatibility shim**, per the call that nothing has launched. An old-format
link is refused rather than accepted, so two spellings of the same link cannot both
survive.

## Refusing quietly was the harder half

`ui-review` blocked on this, and it was right: a rejected link fell back to the
default search in complete silence. The address bar said Seattle → Detroit, one-way,
20 Aug; the page showed Chicago → Paris, round trip, 10 Aug, with nothing to
distinguish it from a first visit. The no-shim decision *creates* that population —
old links are the expected path, not an edge case.

So the page now says the link was not used. Three things fell out of that, each
found by review rather than by me:

- **The notice never cleared.** Reading it straight from the prop meant it survived
  the traveller's own successful search, because the search rewrites the URL with
  `replaceState` and never re-renders the server component — a red banner sitting
  above results that contradict it, the mirror image of the bug being fixed.
- **A refused link still moved the booking window.** The origin is resolved before
  parsing, because the window is what parsing validates dates against; when parsing
  then refused the link, the selectable dates stayed in Tokyo while the form showed
  Chicago. It now comes back to the origin actually on screen.
- **Links refused for their date or cabin fell back silently**, because the check
  gated on `from`/`to` alone.

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 634 unit + 49 database, `npm run

booking-window timezone resolves identically from a code as it did from a label for
all ten origins — measured at 23:56 UTC, when zones straddle the date boundary and
the check is at its most discriminating.

The `verifier` then found **four mutations that survived the whole suite**: the
`?? ''` fallback reinstating the label format, `airportLabelFor` becoming tolerant
of case and whitespace (a shim by the back door), and two ways the refusal notice
could be wrong. The root cause was that `app/page.tsx` had no test, so the predicate
is now an exported function with direct coverage. All four are caught.

It also caught two decayed assertions in my own new e2e: one comparing against
`encodeURIComponent`, which writes `%20` where a query string writes `+`, so it
could never match; and a hard-coded date that would have started passing for the
wrong reason in twelve days.

## Filed rather than fixed

#204 (no visible focus indicator on the search selects), #205 (shared-link arrival
drops focus past the whole form), #206 (return date clipped to `08/17/202`). All
pre-existing, all made more visible by this change, none caused by it.

It finishes the `Flight.from`/`to` work. The issue's typed-statuses task remains:

content.text:
Six issues, and they group naturally. My plan is three slices, worst-first:

1. **Run isolation** (#196 + #173) — the two that make a run untrustworthy in both directions
2. **The two e2e races** (#181, #182)

Starting with the first. Reading the detail:

input.command:

gh issue view 173 --json body -q .body | sed -n 14,60p

result.output:
```

Seat 11A is already taken, so the seat map renders it as occupied and the selector
matching the *selectable* button finds nothing.

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM "SeatAssignment" WHERE "seatNumber" = '11A';  -- 2
```

## Why it is permanent once it happens

`e2e/global-setup.ts` truncates `authRateLimit` and nothing else. Bookings,
passengers, itinerary legs and seat assignments all survive between runs. So the
first run books 11A on the seeded flight and **every subsequent run of those three
specs fails on that database, forever**, until someone reseeds by hand.

This is why the suite passes in CI — CI migrates and seeds a clean database each
time — and rots locally.

## Options

- Have `global-setup.ts` clear the booking tables the way it already clears
  `authRateLimit`. Simple, and matches the existing intent of that file.
- Or have each spec pick a seat that is free at that moment rather than hard-coding
  `11A`, the way `booking.spec.ts` already does for the inbound leg
  (`locator('button[title^="Select Seat"]').nth(1)`).

The first is the better fix: three specs hard-code `11A` today, and a seat chosen at
random makes a failure harder to read.

## Related

This is adjacent to #155, which was the same class of problem inside Jest — tests
sharing one database and interfering with each other. That one was solved by
serialising; this one needs cleanup rather than ordering, because the interference
is between *runs* rather than within one.

content.text: Confirmed pre-existing — it fails on unmodified `main` too, so I didn't cause it. But it makes the suite red, and it's one of the six issues in this cleanup, so I'll fix it here rather than open a PR I know CI may reject:

gh issue view 182 --json body -q .body | sed -n 12,50p

result.output:
```
1629 | 2026-08-08 10:00 | DELAYED
```

inside the board's `now-2h .. now+7d` window, with 29 rows in the window so `take: 200` never truncates. The board simply rendered before the write had committed.

## Mechanism

`components/ui/FlightStatusSelector.tsx` runs `updateFlightStatusAction` inside `startTransition` and then `router.refresh()`. Playwright's `selectOption('DELAYED')` returns as soon as the change event dispatches — it does not wait for the transition. `e2e/admin.spec.ts:239` then navigates straight to `/flights`, which is `force-dynamic` and renders whatever the database holds at that instant.

## Fix

Await the settled state before navigating — the select clearing its `disabled` state, or the row showing the new status on the admin page itself. Asserting the outcome on the page that performed the change is the more honest wait, since that is where the user would see it.

## Related

Same family as #173 and #178: the suite has several waits that assume an action is complete when the DOM event returns.

Found by the `verifier` while checking #195's fix. **Introduced by that fix**, and recorded rather than widened into it.

## Where

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx:37-50`. The poll suppresses `console.error` when the rejection's message is one a browser produces for a torn-down request.

## Why the set is not enough

Those strings are correctly identified, but they are not exclusive to navigation. Verified in real Chromium, none of these involving a navigation:

| Scenario | Message |
|---|---|
| server unreachable | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| connection reset before response | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| server dies mid-body | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| response stream fails mid-read (how React's Flight client consumes a server action) | `TypeError: network error` |

So a crashed, killed or restarting dev server now produces **no console output at all**, where it previously printed every 3 seconds.

input.content:
First of three slices clearing the test-infrastructure tax before Phase 3's ~40 PRs.
Four issues, all of them ways a run could lie about the code under test.

## What each one was

**#196 — a reused dev server.** `reuseExistingServer` borrowed whatever was on the
port. That made a healthy branch fail three runs of three, and the bisect that
followed was worthless: with `webServer: npm run dev`, rebuilding between steps
changes nothing, so every "fix" was really just a server restart. The mirror case is
worse — a stale server can report a pass for code that is not under test. Playwright
now starts its own.

**#173 — seat 11A, held forever.** The suite booked it and nothing released it, so
the seat map rendered it taken and three specs failed on that database from the
first run onwards. CI never saw it because CI seeds a fresh database each time.
Global setup now clears what a previous run booked.

**#182 — navigating before the write landed.** `selectOption` returns on the change
event, not on the server action committing, and `/flights` is `force-dynamic`. The
spec now waits for the change to settle on the page that made it.

**#195 — an aborted poll reported as a failure.** The notification bell polls every
3s; a navigation tears that down. It was the only console error the suite ever
produced.

## Verified by reproduction, not by reading

- Planted the exact leftover #173 describes — 11A held on a seeded flight by a stale
  booking — and the three named specs **failed without the cleanup and passed with
  it**.
- #182 failed 3/3 before the wait and passed 3/3 after. I checked it against
  unmodified `main` first, because I had changed how the server starts and needed to
  rule myself out: it fails there too.
- Two consecutive full green runs, 30/30 each.

## What review caught

`ui-review` found a real defect in my #195 fix. The original matched by regex, and
`/aborted/i` as a substring silenced PostgreSQL's *"current transaction is aborted,
commands ignored until end of transaction block"* and Prisma's *"Transaction
aborted."* — in development Next forwards a server error's message to the client
verbatim, so exactly the failures a developer most needs arrive at that `catch` as
written. It now matches whole messages against a closed set of what browsers
actually say. Whole-message equality is what makes it safe.

The `verifier` then found the new test **green against code that does not do the
job**: it inlined `booking.deleteMany()` rather than calling the function, so
deleting the call from `global-setup.ts` left it passing. Its "seeded inventory
survives" assertions were vacuous too — `flight.count() > 0` is guaranteed by the
fixture the test creates itself. It now imports the real function, counts before and
after, and asserts to the row. Both mutants die.

It also caught that the config assertion pinned source text, so reintroducing reuse
*conditionally* slipped past. It reads the loaded config now.

I removed one of my own tests outright: it asserted a property of whatever the
database happened to hold, and failed when a Playwright run was in progress — a
flake, in a PR about removing flakes.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 643 unit + 51 database, `npm run
build`, and Playwright 30/30 twice.

## One behaviour change worth knowing

A dev server already on port 3000 now **stops** the suite instead of being borrowed:

```
Error: http://localhost:3000 is already used, make sure that nothing is running
on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.
```

It exits in ~2.9s rather than hanging. `AGENTS.md` is updated, since it still said
Playwright auto-starts the server. Note the message advises the setting the config
now forbids — the reason is in the comment beside it.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#212** — the #195 fix means a *dead* dev server now fails silently too. The
  message cannot carry the signal; an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup can.
  Recorded rather than widened into this slice.
- **#213** — `travelguide.spec.ts` leaks a user, review and favorite per run; 37
  accounts had accumulated. Same class as #173, not covered by it.
- **#208, #209, #210, #211** — pre-existing notification-bell findings from
  `ui-review`: the drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone, the empty state
  claims "You're all caught up!" when loading failed, the unread count is invisible
  to assistive tech, and `next-auth`'s own session poll still logs on hard
  navigation.

## Still to come

#181 (search e2e reads a stale return date) and #178 (round-trip e2e headroom) are
the next slice; #165 is housekeeping after that.

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app
gh issue create --title "Database test serialisation depends on how Jest is invoked, not on the config" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found while addressing Codex review on #214 — by tripping over it repeatedly.

## Where

`package.json:15` — `"test:database": "npx jest --selectProjects database --runInBand"`.

`jest.config.js` splits the projects and documents at length why the database files must not run beside each other, but the config itself does not enforce it. `--runInBand` in the npm script is the only thing that serialises them.

## What was observed

Running `npx jest --selectProjects database` directly — which looks equivalent, and which the config's own comment does not warn against — runs those files in parallel. That reproduces exactly the interference #155 was filed for:

```
● the route a page renders › comes from the airports on the admin dashboard
  Expected substring: "RTE-66f9eabc"
```

`runIsolation.database.test.ts` calls `clearPreviousRunBookings()`, which deletes every booking by design, while `routeRenderSources.database.test.ts` is holding a fixture booking open. Intermittent: it passed on the immediately following run.

Verified: `npm run test:database` passes 3 runs of 3.

## Why it matters

The split exists so a whole-table assertion cannot count another file's fixtures. That guarantee currently holds only if you type the right command — and the wrong command is the shorter, more obvious one. It cost me several confusing failures in one session, each of which looked like a real regression in the code under review.

`jest` does not support a per-project `maxWorkers`, so the fix is not a one-liner. Options worth weighing: a `globalSetup` for the database project that refuses to run when it detects parallelism; a top-level `maxWorkers: 1` (correct but slows the 64-suite unit project); or a `testSequencer`/wrapper that makes the direct invocation fail loudly with a pointer to the script.

Related: #155 (the original collisions), and the note in `AGENTS.md` under Gotchas that already tells agents to use the scripts.
EOF
)" --label roadmap 2>&1 | tail -1

   **Codex reviews every pull request, and its verdict is a merge gate.** It
   runs on the pull request rather than the working tree, so this loop belongs
   after step 10 has opened one. Do not merge until it approves.

   - It reacts 👀 on the pull request while it is reading, and posts inline
     review comments if it finds anything. When it is satisfied it removes the
     👀 and reacts 👍. Both reactions are on the **pull request itself**, not on
     a comment: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<pr>/reactions`.
   - Its findings are inline review threads, not issue comments. They are
     invisible to `gh pr view --json comments`; read them with
     `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<pr>/comments`, or through GraphQL
     `reviewThreads` when you need the thread IDs to resolve them.
   - Every push re-triggers it. So the loop is: address the findings, run the
     tests, push, reply to each thread saying what changed and why, resolve
     the thread, then wait for the next verdict. Repeat until 👍.
   - Reply before resolving, and say what you actually did. A resolved thread
     with no reply is indistinguishable from one dismissed without reading.
     Where a finding is right about the problem but wrong about the fix, say
     so and explain what you did instead — and where you disagree, say that
     too rather than resolving quietly.
   - Findings carry a priority badge. Treat P1 as blocking. It is worth
     arguing with: three rounds on #214 turned a hostname check into an
     environment marker because each round rejected the previous fix for a
     concrete reason, and each rejection was correct.
   - Do not confuse your own replies with a new review. Replying creates
     review objects under your name; only a review by
     `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` **on the current head SHA** is a verdict.
   - `@codex review` in a comment re-triggers it without a push, for when a
     round needed no code change.
